What is a hash function?
A hash function is a mathematical algorithm that converts input data (any size) into fixed-length hash values.
Is hashing the same as encryption?
No. Hashing is one-way (irreversible); encryption is two-way (reversible with a key).
What is MD5?
MD5 produces 128-bit (32 hex char) hashes. Now cryptographically broken; avoid for security-critical applications.
What is SHA1?
SHA1 produces 160-bit hashes (40 hex chars). Has known vulnerabilities; deprecated for security applications.
What is SHA256?
SHA256 produces 256-bit hashes (64 hex chars). Part of SHA-2, considered secure for most applications.
What is SHA512?
SHA512 produces 512-bit hashes (128 hex chars). Part of SHA-2, stronger than SHA256.
Why use hash functions?
Uses include: verify data integrity, create digital signatures, password storage, detect tampering.
Can I reverse a hash?
No. Cryptographic hashes are designed to be one-way (irreversible). You cannot get original data from hash.
Why hash passwords?
Hashing protects passwords: if databases are breached, actual passwords remain secret (attackers get hashes).
What is a salt?
A salt is random data added before hashing. Prevents identical hashes and rainbow table attacks.
Can different inputs produce the same hash?
Theoretically yes (collision), but cryptographic functions make this computationally infeasible.
Is this generator secure for production passwords?
For learning yes. For production, use dedicated password hashing: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2.
